question: Why is storing a growing per-user map in Instance storage a denial-of-service risk in Soroban?

golden.answer: Instance storage lives in the contract-instance ledger entry, which is loaded whole on every invocation. A growing per-user map raises every call's cost and eventually hits resource or entry-size limits, so growth-dependent paths fail. An over-limit write fails atomically and prior state is kept: a DoS risk, not an automatic permanent brick. The size limit is validator-voted and can be lowered, so leave headroom. Keep Instance small; shard per-user data into Persistent keys.
keyFacts: Instance storage is one ledger entry loaded in full on every invocation.
Unbounded Instance growth raises every call's cost and can hit entry-size limits.
An over-limit write fails atomically and prior valid state is preserved.
Per-user or growing data belongs in separate, sharded Persistent keys.
avoid: Do NOT call the first over-limit write an irreversible permanent brick.
Do NOT say Instance storage loads lazily like separate Persistent keys.
golden.notes: An instance entry left above a later-lowered validator-voted size limit failing every call is correct, not a brick claim.

truth.notes:
Routes to scout_research (security corpus). Instance = whole instance entry loaded per call; verified against the storage/state-archival semantics. Trap: thinking Instance loads lazily.
Also good if the answer: This is a recognized Soroban vulnerability class (Instance-storage DoS / unbounded storage growth) in audit checklists.
Golden cites: A Soroban security checklist (e.g., Veridise) or developers.stellar.org storage guidance.
GT-46 CORRECTION 2026-07-11: distinguish rejected writes and growth-path DoS from an unsupported permanent-brick claim.
2026-11-02 read-path qualifier: stellar-core validates contract-data entry size on footprint reads as well as writes. An answer that says an instance entry left above a later-lowered contract_data_entry_size_bytes makes every call fail until the limit is raised is correct and does not fire avoid[0]. An answer that says ordinary growth makes the existing entry unreadable or the contract permanently unusable is still wrong.
